text: Monitoring and alerting only prove their worth during an actual incident. This lesson runs a game-day drill that reproduces a real flash-sale outage against the infrastructure you built in Phases 1 through 3, and diagnoses it using the exact dashboards and SLO from Lesson 14.

A load-testing job ramps synthetic checkout traffic against northbridge-staging to flash-sale volume, and checkout's p99 latency climbs on the Grafana dashboard from a roughly 400 millisecond baseline toward 6.2 seconds. Request rate stays flat while duration climbs, which is the first clue that the problem isn't inside checkout's own code at all.

That clue sends you to the USE method, applied to the real bottleneck: the legacy inventory service's database connection pool. Utilization versus pool max and wait-queue depth both show saturation — the pool was undersized and had never been load-tested for flash-sale volume, so every checkout request waiting on a stock check queued behind it.

The damage adds up fast. Checkout's p99 latency stayed above 2 seconds for 34 minutes, affecting an estimated 4,100 customer sessions and 220 abandoned carts above baseline. Only a full-exhaustion alert existed on the inventory pool, so it fired after the queue had already built, and the on-call runbook never pointed at inventory as a suspect — costing about 12 minutes of live trace discovery before anyone found the actual cause.

The postmortem stays blameless — it asks what in the system allowed this, never who caused it — and every action item gets a real owner and a real date: a saturation-based alert on the inventory pool's wait-queue depth, a circuit breaker so checkout degrades gracefully instead of hanging, and a larger, load-tested connection pool before the next scheduled flash sale.

That's the whole loop closed: an incident, diagnosed with your own monitoring stack, resolved with owned fixes instead of blame. Next lesson wraps the technical build with documentation and a presentation script before the capstone moves into Career Prep.
